# SK2052 — The shift count is masked to a different count

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A shift's constant count is outside the range of its promoted left operand's width, so C# masks it and the expression shifts by a different amount.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| ReSharper | `ShiftExpressionRealShiftCountIsZero` (`resharper_shift_expression_real_shift_count_is_zero_highlighting`) |

## Why

⚠ C# masks a shift count, it does not clamp it: `x << 32` on an `int` shifts by `32 & 31`, which is zero, so the expression is the identity rather than the zero almost everybody expects. On a `long` the mask is 63, so the same text is a genuine 32-bit shift. The rule therefore has to know the promoted width of the left operand and cannot be decided from syntax — a `byte` left operand promotes to `int` and masks with 31. There is no fix: rewriting `x << 33` to `x << 1` preserves the defect while making it look deliberate, and widening the operand guesses an intent the rule cannot read.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
int mask = value << 32;
```

Write:

```csharp
long mask = (long)value << 32;
```

## When it does not fire

Only built-in, non-lifted `<<`, `>>` and `>>>` whose result type is exactly `int`, `uint`, `long` or `ulong` are considered. ⚠ `nint` and `nuint` are excluded because their shift mask is 31 or 63 depending on the process, so the same source is correct on one platform and not the other and no single answer is right. A count already inside the width — including a literal `<< 0`, which is redundant but not masked — is not reported; only a count that the mask actually changes is. A constant zero left operand is reported separately as a result that is always zero, and only when the count is not itself constant, so that a fully constant expression the compiler already folded is not reported twice. Range-derived findings — a shift whose result is zero because the left operand's known values are too small — are outside this initial scope, and so are user-defined shift operators.
